newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. rights report sees Indian concerns - analysts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rights report sees Indian concerns - analysts.

text.p: The United States' annual human rights report released last week signals a growing sensitivity to Indian concerns that separatist militants must share the blame for rights violations, analysts said at the weekend.

A change of attitude in Washington could be directly linked to the U.S. experience in dealing with the abduction of four Western hostages in the troubled Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir, a politicial analyst said.
"Ever since the Western hostages were kidnapped, the U.S. government has changed," said Brahma Chellaney of the Centre for Policy Research, referring to their abduction in July 1995.

The State Department, in its 20th annual human rights report of 193 countries, said on Thursday there continued to be significant human rights violations in India despite constitutional and legal safeguards. But it said separatist militants were also responsible for numerous serious rights abuses.

One American is still hostage after another escaped after the kidnappings by mysterious Al-Faran guerrillas in Kashmir, which has often been the focus of reports on suspected human rights violations in India.
Besides the American, two Britons and a German are still missing, despite occasional reports of sightings.
The beheaded body of a fifth hostage, a Norwegian, was found in August 1995 in a remote Kashmiri forest.

India often blames separatists for carrying out kidnappings, extortion and acts of violence, and Indian critics have in the past said Washington singled out New Delhi while ignoring its difficulties in troubled areas like Kashmir.
Human rights issues have been a major irritant in relations between the world's two largest democracies.

"The militant part is not something new. But the emphasis is now stronger on militants. The nuances are important," Chellaney said. "They are becoming more stridently critical of the role of the militants. The latest report only reflects the trend."
An Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman offered no comment on the State Department report.
But another official, who asked not to be identified, said India discerned a change in the U.S. attitude. "One has to see it in the light of what they have been seeing in the past," he said.

Y.S. Chhibbar, general secretary of India's People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL), said New Delhi's track record in human rights improved after the government set up a National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in 1994.
"After the establishment of the NHRC, our government's attitude has definitely changed," Chhibbar said. "Before that, they used to call us (activists) foreign agents," he said.
"NHRC now looks into matters and they have gone to investigate some things in Kashmir which by law is outside their jurisdiction," he added.

From the U.S. side, the mention of rights violations by guerrillas added to the credibility of the State Department, he said, adding "not many people are willing" to consider rights abuses by guerrillas.
Indian officials often accuse neighbouring Pakistan of arming guerrillas in the Himalayan region where violence has claimed more than 20,000 lives since a separatist revolt began in 1990.
Pakistan, which has fought two wars with India over Kashmir, denies the accusations and says it provides only moral and diplomatic support to the guerrillas.
